hook1.text: A car loan with $25,000 left at 5.2%.

hook2.text: pay it off early, or invest the extra cash.

hook3.text: We ran both roads through all 48 months, taxing every lot.

hook4.text: The answer flips at an average annual return of 6.11% compounded in the 22% tax bracket.

hook5.text: Below it, paying off ends ahead. Above it, investing does.

scope1.text: Here is the setup. The rules are US tax rules, and every input is stated, not forecast.

scope2.text: Loan interest is treated as not deductible, so the model ignores the new car loan interest deduction for 2025 to 2028.

facts.text: The loan has $25,000 left at 5.2% with 48 monthly payments of $578.

extra.text: On top of that, $400 a month is available. That amount is illustrative.

roads.text: Road A sends it to the loan. Road B pays the minimum and invests it every month.

cash.text: Both roads spend the same cash each month. Only the order changes.

timeline.text: Road A pays off the loan at month 28. Road B keeps paying for month 48.

free.text: That leaves 20 months with no car payment on road A.

avoided.text: Road A avoids $1,190 of interest. That does not depend on markets or taxes.

identity.text: Because both roads spend the same cash, Road A ends up investing exactly $1,190 more than Road B.

bridge.text: So, the question is narrow. Can road B's head start in the market beat a certain $1,190 after tax?

lots1.text: Each month's contribution is its own tax lot. At month 48, everything is sold.

lots2.text: A lot held more than 12 months at that sale is long-term. The rest are short-term.

rates.text: In the 22% bracket, long-term gains are taxed at 15% and short-term gains at the full 22%.

lots3.text: Road B invests from the start, so 35 of its 48 lots are long-term. Road A starts after the payoff, 8 of its 21.

share.text: Near the break-even, 37% of road A's gains are short-term against 7% of road B's.

nodeduct.text: A lot that loses money gets no deduction. State income tax is left out.

sw1.text: We sweep the average annual return from 2% to 10%, compounded in the 22% bracket.

sw2.text: The line is ROAD B minus ROAD A, net worth after tax at month 48, and it rises with the return.

sw3.text: At 2%, Road A is ahead by $822. At 10%, Road B is ahead by $861.

sw5.text: Below that return, paying off early ends ahead. Above it, investing does.

niit.text: In the 32% bracket, we add the 3.8% net investment income tax. Short-term gains pay 35.8%, long-term gains 18.8%.

dots.text: The break even is 5.23% in the 12% bracket and 6.11% in the 22% bracket.

rises.text: Higher rates on games shrink road B's head start. So the threshold rises with the bracket.

below.text: In the 12% bracket, it sits below 5.33%. The loan rate has an annual yield because road A's gains are mostly short-term.

risk1.text: paying off the loan earns a certain 5.2 percent.

risk2.text: Investing earns an average, not a promise. Our range, 2% to 10%, is illustrative.

seq.text: Here is an illustrative sequence. 8% a year for 36 months, then minus 20% for the last 12.

race.text: We track net worth after tax, month by month. For 36 months, both roads run almost together.

gap.text: The difference, road B minus road A, peaks, then turns negative in month 39.

downside.text: Road A finishes $459.00 ahead after tax.

order.text: Over all 48 months, that sequence still averages 0.19% a year. The order of the returns decided the result.

recap.text: The payoff month and the interest avoided are fixed. The tax depends on how long each lot is held. The return is the unknown.

end1.text: So, in the 22% bracket, the answer flips at an average annual return of 6.11%.

end2.text: That is a threshold, not a forecast. Where returns will land, is not known in advance.
